newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Inflation seen posing few EMU worries for Portugal.
newsitem.headline: Inflation seen posing few EMU worries for Portugal.

text.p: The Portuguese government has set itself an ambitious inflation goal for the 1997 budget, but even if it misses the target it could still meet the prices condition for economic and monetary union (EMU), economists say.
Prime Minister Antonio Guterres's Socialist administration wants inflation down by December next year to 2.25-2.50 percent from a forecast 3.0 percent at the end of 1996.
The rate, calculated on the basis of a rolling 12-month average, stood at 3.3 percent in August this year.
"We don't see inflation as a problem (for Portugal) even if 2.5 percent is ambitious and it may not be as low as that," said Mario Diaz Vigario of Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.
Analysts forecast the average inflation rate would be between 2.5 percent and 3.0 percent by the end of 1997.

But even at 3.0 percent, the rate should still be good enough for Portugal to meet one of the most rigidly-defined of the entry qualifications for the European Union's (EU) planned single currency, analysts said.

While the wording of the EMU debt and deficit tests leave some room for interpretation when the EU decides who qualifies and who does not at the start of 1998, the inflation target is inflexible, economists say.
Nations opting to join EMU must have an average inflation rate at the end of 1997 that is no more than 1.5 percent above the average of the EU's three best-performers.
"On our numbers, they are going to be inside (the EMU limit)," said UBS economist Sally Wilkinson.
Wilkinson said that UBS was working on a cut-off for EMU of 3.2 percent, with the average of the three countries with the lowest inflation being 1.7 percent.

The government, which is committed to joining a single currency when it is launched in 1999 if it can, is drawing up a budget for next year designed to meet the EMU deficit standard of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP). The 1996 deficit is forecast at around four percent.
Portugal has no chance of getting its state debt, currently around 70 percent of GDP, inside the 60 percent ceiling but then neither has Belgium, often mentioned as an EMU certainty.
Crucial to a further decline in inflation next year will be the outcome of coming wage negotiations and the performance of the Portuguese escudo on the foreign exchanges, economists say.
Barring some international crisis, they see little cause for concern on the currency front.

Any problems that could come from a strengthening dollar -- higher prices for raw material imports -- would be shared equally by all EU countries and so should not complicate Portugal's task of being inside the inflation ceiling.

Banco Portugues de Investimento (BPI) chief economist Rui Martins dos Santos said that he expected Portugal's tradable inflation rate, which measures prices of internationally commercialised goods and services, to be in line with its major EU partners at some two percent next year.
The key ingredient of non-tradable prices will be the level of wage rises for next year to be agreed at coming talks between the unions and the government.

The government has said that there is room for only very small increases above the programmed inflation rate. Past experience suggests that unions will eventually settle for real rises -- after inflation -- of 0.5-1.0 percent, economists say.
For Fincor economist Isabel Cabral, an inflation rate of 2.5 percent next year would need wage rises to be held below 3.0 percent overall next year.

The work of the forecasters has been slightly complicated by the fact that the National Statistics Institute (INE) changes its the base for calculating the consumer price index with effect from 1997 to bring it more into line with the European Commission's standard.
"If the index were the same, we were forecasting 2.7 percent but we do not know what the impact of the changes will be," said Dos Santos.
